addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## agent-ml-research
ML research experiment management tools

attachment.content:
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion

We validated OntoCoDec across 2 RE datasets, 3 model families, and event extraction (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
The central finding is non-additive layer interaction: grammar alone achieves 3\% DR reduction on SciERC, semantic alone 24\%, but their composition yields 94\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results})---grammar-enforced vocabulary membership creates the clean input the semantic layer requires.

\paragraph{Scale-dependent layer interaction.}
This dependency weakens at scale: at 70B, the semantic layer independently achieves 84\% DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
We offer a speculative hypothesis: larger models exhibit improved vocabulary calibration, assigning higher probability to ontology-valid tokens and reducing the semantic layer's dependence on grammar-enforced vocabulary membership (Appendix~\ref{app:causal-tracing}); confirming this causal mechanism requires cross-family verification beyond our current scope.
Fallback frequency varies dramatically across architectures (0 vs.\ 5{,}882 under LoRA+S1) without affecting enforcement (both DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\%), confirming grammar is necessary but increasingly insufficient as models improve.
Constraint enforcement is preserved under INT4 quantization (Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}).

\paragraph{DR$\leftrightarrow$CF trade-off.}
Greedy S1 reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.21\% but introduces CF (zero-shot $+$9.82\,pp, fine-tuned $+$1.18\,pp)---an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement.
Among 248 zero-shot CF violations, 58.1\% involve hallucinated entities (absent from gold) and only 7.3\% are true cascade errors (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); fine-tuned CF drops to $\leq$1.4\%.
Beam $k{=}2$ reduces CF to 0.11\% at 1.18$\times$ latency (Pareto-optimal; recommended for zero-shot deployment); $k{=}4$ eliminates all violations at 8B at 1.39$\times$ (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).

\paragraph{Complementarity and deployment.}
GoLLIE and KnowCoder internalize schema knowledge via training but lack runtime guarantees; LoRA + S1 shows the two are complementary (DR 1--2\%\,$\to$\,$\leq$0.21\%).
S2 (two-pass) degrades at 70B ($-$8\,pp R-F1), consistent with CRANE~\cite{banerjee2025crane}; we recommend S1 as default.
The root cause---per-triple enforcement cannot coordinate cross-triple type assignments (Level~3; \S\ref{sec:decidability})---requires global entity-level consensus beyond online masking; beam search and TCR approximate this, with full integration as future work.

1	\section{Related Work}
2	\label{sec:related_work}
3	
4	We provide a detailed survey in Appendix~\ref{app:related_work}; here we position OntoCoDec along three axes.
5	
6	\paragraph{Constrained decoding.}
7	XGrammar~\cite{dong2025xgrammar}, Outlines~\cite{willard2023outlines}, SynCode~\cite{ugare2024syncode}, SGLang~\cite{zheng2024sglang}, and related systems~\cite{beurer-kellner2023lmql,park2024grammar,jsonschemabench2025} enforce format validity via CFG-based token masking but lack cross-field semantic awareness.
8	PICARD~\cite{scholak2021picard} and \citet{pldi2025_type_constrained_codegen} compile type systems into prefix automata; KG-Trie~\cite{luo2025kgtrie} applies trie-based KG constraints during decoding for knowledge-to-text generation.
9	Unlike PICARD, which operates over a fixed, fully enumerated SQL schema with statically declared column types, OntoCoDec's entity registry is populated dynamically during generation as entity spans are extracted from free text, requiring prefix-decidable enforcement rather than context-free lookup.
10	
11	\paragraph{Schema-aware IE.}
12	GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie}, KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}, and others~\cite{guidex2025,josifoski2022genie,paolini2021tanl,cabot2021rebel,wang2023instructuie,qi2024adelie,fei2022lasuie,lu2022uie,zhou2024universalner} encode ontology structure via training-time internalization without runtime enforcement~\cite{wadhwa2023revisiting}.
13	GoLLIE achieves schema compliance through annotation-guideline-guided generation at training time (reporting 63.6--70.1\% RE F1 on ACE05 in supervised settings; SciERC RE not evaluated); OntoCoDec provides orthogonal runtime enforcement, composable with any generative IE system including GoLLIE itself (Appendix~\ref{app:gollie-comparison}).
14	
15	\paragraph{Constraint enforcement in IE.}
16	\citet{roth_yih_2004} and \citet{riedel2010modeling} formulated hard type constraints via integer linear programming (ILP); post-hoc validation~\cite{khorshidi2025odke,spires_2024,ontologx_2025} detects violations after generation but discards up to 74\% of predictions.
17	EnriCo~\cite{zaratiana2024enrico} uses answer set programming (ASP); IterGen~\cite{ugare2025itergen} backtracks on violations; \citet{vukovic2024dialogue} combines ontology constraints with constrained chain-of-thought for dialogue RE---OntoCoDec uses forward-only masking at $O(|V|)$ per step without iterative refinement.
18	Grammar-only enforcement (GCD~\cite{geng2023gcd}, BoostCD~\cite{boostcd2025}) achieves only 3\% DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:constrained-baselines}).
19

For constrained decoding, I'll group XGrammar, Outlines, SynCode and similar systems together since they all use CFG-based masking but lack semantic awareness. Then I'll mention PICARD and the type-system approaches, followed by what makes OntoCoDec distinct—the dynamic entity registry and prefix-decidable enforcement. For schema-aware IE, I'm starting to list GoLLIE, KnowCoder and others, so I'll continue positioning those systems and then differentiate OntoCoDec's approach. I'm looking at how existing approaches handle constraint enforcement in information extraction—some use post-hoc validation that discards a significant portion of predictions, others employ answer set programming or backtracking when violations occur, and a few combine ontology constraints with chain-of-thought reasoning for dialogue tasks. OntoCoDec takes a different approach with forward-only masking that's computationally efficient, and grammar-only enforcement methods show minimal improvements compared to what we're achieving.

Now I'm defining the formal structure of an IE ontology, which specifies entity types, relation types, and the valid type pairs allowed for each relation. A key metric here is constraint tightness—how restrictive the constraints are in limiting valid type combinations per relation.

OntoCoDec merges both formal ontology specifications and empirically derived constraints from annotated data, achieving over 99% instance-level coverage while maintaining a grammar-first fallback to ensure no valid triples get incorrectly filtered.

Grammar-constrained decoding works by masking each generated token to only valid options based on a target grammar. Tools like XGrammar, Outlines, and SGLang compile JSON Schemas into pushdown automata to enforce structural validity.

However, these systems are limited to context-free constraints and can't enforce cross-field semantic rules—like requiring the head entity type to be Method or OtherScientificTerm when the relation is Feature-of. I'm now formulating the core problem: given an ontology and a language model, I need constraints that guarantee both structural validity (well-formed JSON with proper entity and relation membership) and type validity (ensuring every triple's head and tail types match the relation's allowed type pairs).

The first condition is context-free and straightforward, but the second is context-sensitive yet prefix-decidable—meaning by the time I generate a type token, I already have all the information I need from the decoded prefix, as long as each entity type name maps to a distinguishable token sequence.

At 8B parameters, grammar alone cuts decoding rate by 3%, semantics alone by 24%, but together they achieve 94%—the grammar layer provides clean input that the semantic layer depends on. However, this interaction weakens at scale: at 70B, semantics independently reaches 84% reduction, and while fallback frequency varies wildly across architectures without breaking enforcement, the grammar constraint becomes increasingly unnecessary as models improve. The enforcement itself holds up under INT4 quantization.

There's a trade-off between decoding rate and constraint feasibility: greedy decoding reduces decoding rate to under 0.21% but introduces constraint violations. I'm consolidating the key findings: beam search with k=2 achieves near-zero constraint violations at minimal latency cost, while the complementarity analysis shows that per-triple enforcement fundamentally can't coordinate across triples—requiring either beam search, TCR, or global entity-level consensus for full correctness.

lines: An IE ontology $\mathcal{O} = (\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{R}, \sigma)$ defines entity types $\mathcal{E}$, relation types $\mathcal{R}$, and a mapping $\sigma: \mathcal{R} \to \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{E} \times \mathcal{E})$, where $\mathcal{P}(\cdot)$ denotes the power set, specifying valid (head type, tail type) pairs per relation.
A triple $(h, r, t)$ is \emph{type-valid} if $(\mathrm{type}(h), \mathrm{type}(t)) \in \sigma(r)$.
We quantify constraint restrictiveness via \emph{constraint tightness} $\kappa(r)$ (\S\ref{sec:composition}): tighter constraints leave fewer valid type pairs per relation.

-We define ontology constraints broadly to encompass both formal ontology specifications (e.g., the KAIROS event ontology with explicit role-entity type mappings) and empirically derived type-pair constraints extracted from annotated training data.
-The latter applies when datasets lack a formal ontology but provide typed annotations (SciERC, DocRED); OntoCoDec compiles both sources into the same constraint representation without modification.

-Empirical constraints achieve 99\%+ instance-level coverage on held-out data (SciERC 99.0\%, DocRED 99.4\%); uncovered type pairs trigger grammar-first fallback (\S\ref{sec:composition}), ensuring no valid triples are blocked.

+OntoCoDec compiles both formal ontology specifications and empirically derived type-pair constraints from annotated data into the same representation; empirical constraints achieve 99\%+ instance-level coverage (SciERC 99.0\%, DocRED 99.4\%), with grammar-first fallback (\S\ref{sec:composition}) ensuring no valid triples are blocked.
\paragraph{Grammar-Constrained Decoding.}
\label{sec:bg:gcd}
Grammar-constrained decoding restricts each token $y_t$ to a mask $M_g \in \{0, 1\}^{|V|}$ derived from a target grammar.

-XGrammar~\citep{dong2025xgrammar} compiles JSON Schemas into pushdown automata for efficient enforcement of structural constraints; Outlines~\citep{willard2023outlines} and SGLang~\citep{zheng2024sglang} offer similar capabilities.

-However, these methods are limited to context-free constraints and cannot enforce cross-field semantic rules (e.g., ``if $r$ = \textsc{Feature-of}, then $\mathrm{type}(h) \in \{\textsc{Method}, \textsc{OtherScientificTerm}\}$''), which depend on previously generated field values.

% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion

We validated OntoCoDec across 2 RE datasets, 3 model families, and event extraction (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
The central finding is non-additive layer interaction: grammar alone achieves 3\% DR reduction, semantic alone 24\%, but their composition yields 94\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results})---grammar-enforced vocabulary membership creates the clean input the semantic layer requires.

\paragraph{Scale-dependent layer interaction.}
This dependency weakens at scale: at 70B, the semantic layer independently achieves 84\% DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
Fallback frequency varies dramatically across architectures (0 vs.\ 5{,}882 under LoRA+S1) without affecting enforcement (both DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\%), confirming grammar is necessary but increasingly insufficient as models improve (Appendix~\ref{app:causal-tracing}).
Constraint enforcement is preserved under INT4 quantization (Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}).

\paragraph{DR$\leftrightarrow$CF trade-off.}
Greedy S1 reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.21\% but introduces CF (zero-shot $+$9.82\,pp, fine-tuned $+$1.18\,pp)---an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement.
Beam $k{=}2$ reduces CF to 0.11\% at 1.18$\times$ latency (Pareto-optimal; recommended for zero-shot deployment); $k{=}4$ eliminates all violations at 8B at 1.39$\times$ (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).

\paragraph{Complementarity and deployment.}
GoLLIE and KnowCoder internalize schema knowledge via training but lack runtime guarantees; LoRA + S1 shows complementarity (DR 1--2\%\,$\to$\,$\leq$0.21\%).
S2 degrades at 70B ($-$8\,pp R-F1); we recommend S1 as default.
The root cause---per-triple enforcement cannot coordinate cross-triple type assignments (Level~3; \S\ref{sec:decidability})---requires global entity-level consensus; beam search and TCR approximate this, with full integration as future work.

\begin{abstract}
Large language models (LLMs) for information extraction (IE) generate structurally valid but ontologically invalid triples---where entity types violate the ontology's domain/range constraints.
These violations persist across the capability spectrum and cannot be addressed by grammar-constrained decoding (which lacks cross-field type awareness) or post-hoc filtering (which discards valid predictions).
We present \textsc{OntoCoDec} (\textbf{Onto}logy-\textbf{Co}mpiled \textbf{Dec}oding), a framework that compiles IE ontologies into composable token-level decoding constraints.
A decidability analysis shows that domain/range constraints exceed context-free expressiveness, yielding a two-layer architecture: a grammar layer enforces structural validity and vocabulary membership; a semantic layer enforces type constraints at runtime through stateful masking over a dynamic entity registry.
% exp_ids: w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval
Evaluated across three 8B-class models and two relation extraction datasets (up to 96 relations), OntoCoDec composed with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning reduces domain/range (DR) violations to $\leq$\,0.21\% at F1 40--46\% ($\pm$0.3 percentage points vs.\ unconstrained), converting irrecoverable type errors to correctable cross-field (CF) inconsistencies (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\%); beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types at 8B at ${\sim}$1.5$\times$ latency.
97.6--100\% of enforcement-removed triples are false positives.
In zero-shot settings, DR reductions span 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED; CF increases are concentrated in hallucinated entities (58.1\%) and decrease with scale and fine-tuning.
\end{abstract}

1	% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)
2	
3	\section{Introduction}
4	\label{sec:introduction}
5	
6	Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for information extraction (IE)~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
7	We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
8	Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates follow an observed pattern consistent with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
9	At competitive quality (Relation F1 (R-F1) 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.
10	
11	Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
12	Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on SciERC but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for information extraction (IE)~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates follow an observed pattern consistent with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At competitive quality (Relation F1 (R-F1) 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on SciERC but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering discards up to 74\% of predictions including true positives (Appendices~\ref{app:cross-model-zs},~\ref{app:posthoc-extended}).
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (CFGs) (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with a scale-dependent layer interaction: at 8B, the semantic layer achieves only 24\% independent DR reduction (near-complete when combined), while at 70B it reaches 84\% independently.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), three 8B-class models across three tokenizer families, with 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
LoRA + greedy S1 reduces DR to near-zero: DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\% at R-F1 40--46\% ($\pm$0.3\,pp, $+$10\% latency); 97.6--100\% of removed triples are false positives (\S\ref{sec:downstream-impact}). Beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types at 8B on both RE datasets (${\sim}$1.5$\times$ latency).
DR enforcement converts ontologically invalid violations to individually valid but type-inconsistent ones (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned); zero-shot DR drops 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED, with total violations (DR+CF) decreasing 30--51\% (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).

OntoCoDec is a constraint enforcement method, orthogonal and complementary to training-based schema-aware approaches such as GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}; it can be composed with any generative IE system to improve schema compliance without retraining.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_scale_dependency.pdf}
\caption{Scale-dependent layer interaction: the semantic layer's independent DR reduction grows from 24\% at 8B to 84\% at 70B, reducing reliance on grammar-enforced vocabulary.}
\label{fig:scale-dependency}
\end{figure}

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item An empirical finding of non-additive layer interaction: grammar-only constraints reduce domain-range violations by 3\% and semantic-only by 24\%, but their composition achieves 94\%---revealing an enabling dependency where grammar-enforced vocabulary membership creates the clean input the semantic layer requires.
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework showing that domain/range type constraints require stateful enforcement beyond context-free grammars---grammar-only approaches face state spaces of $6^{17}$--$6^{19}$ for typical IE schemas (Proposition~1; \S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from IE ontologies, validated on schemas with up to 96 relation types.
    \item Evidence of scale-dependent layer interaction on Llama-3.1-70B (AWQ INT4): the semantic layer alone achieves 84\% DR reduction at 70B vs.\ 24\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}). At 8B, beam $k{=}2$ is Pareto-optimal (R-F1 44.60, CF 0.11\%, 1.18$\times$ greedy S1 latency); $k{=}4$ achieves DR${=}$0\% with near-zero CF at 1.39$\times$.
\end{enumerate}

1	% Section: Constraint Composition (compressed, 787→~500 words)
2	
3	At each decoding step $t$, let $G(t) \subseteq V$ and $S(t) \subseteq V$ denote the tokens permitted by the grammar and semantic layers, respectively.
4	The final mask is their conjunction:
5	%
6	\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
7	  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
8	\end{equation}
9	%
10	where $\wedge$ denotes element-wise AND over the vocabulary $V$; a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.
11	The conjunction is asymmetric: $S(t)$ is defined only over $G(t)$. This reflects the scale-dependent layer interaction (\S\ref{sec:method}): the semantic layer requires the relation type to belong to $\mathcal{R}$, a property enforced only by the grammar layer.
12	This dependency is scale-sensitive: 70B semantic-only achieves 84\% DR reduction (vs.\ 24\% on 8B), though grammar remains necessary for RV elimination (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
13	
14	\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}
15	When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ (tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid), na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
16	We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback}: semantic masking is skipped and the grammar layer alone controls selection.
17	Structural integrity is a hard constraint; type violations are soft errors detectable by downstream validation, with DR (ontologically invalid type pair) more severe than CF (individually valid triples with cross-triple type inconsistency).
18	Extraction tasks are robust to format-level constraints~\cite{tam2024letmespeak}, supporting this asymmetric treatment.
19	
20	\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}
21	\label{eq:tightness}
22	Per-relation constraint tightness $\kappa(r) = 1 - |\sigma(r)|/|\mathcal{E}|^2$ captures schema restrictiveness; DR reduction correlates descriptively with schema-mean $\bar{\kappa}$ across our three evaluation schemas ($n{=}3$), though entity type confusability is a significant co-factor (Appendix~\ref{app:kappa-case-study},~\ref{app:tcr}).
23	
24	\paragraph{Greedy limitation and fallback cascade.}
25	\label{sec:greedy-limitation}
26	Single-pass per-triple enforcement cannot coordinate type assignments across triples sharing the same entity mention; cross-field consistency requires global inference that exceeds the per-token masking paradigm.
27	The semantic layer commits entity types greedily---an instance of Level~3 (non-local) constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability})---so CF violations arise when the same entity receives different types across triples; beam search mitigates this (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
28	Fallback triggers on 0.5--5.7\% of type-bearing positions (zero-shot), virtually eliminated by fine-tuning ($\leq$\,0.11\%); all residual DR occurs at fallback positions (Appendix~\ref{app:causal-tracing}).
29	
30	\paragraph{Non-rectangularity and independent enforcement.}
31	\label{sec:rectangularity}
32	Type signatures are non-rectangular (0/7 SciERC, 23/96 DocRED rectangular); independent enforcement admits 33--37\% spurious pairs, eliminated by fine-tuning (Table~\ref{tab:composability}).
33	Shuffling type order produces byte-identical outputs across all 551 SciERC documents, confirming order invariance (Appendix~\ref{app:order-invariance}).
34

DR-to-CF conversion represents a severity downgrade: DR is irrecoverable without re-extraction, while CF---individually valid triples with cross-triple inconsistency---is amenable to post-hoc resolution (type consistency reranking (TCR) eliminates all CF in our experiments, with bounded DR regression; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).
Zero-shot evaluation thus establishes violation prevalence and constraint interaction; fine-tuning demonstrates practical elimination.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (e) Composability with Fine-Tuning (expanded)
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
\label{sec:composability}
% exp_ids: bootstrap_ci_ft_composability.json, w5_lora_scierc_*, w8_*
Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 0.5--2\% but leaves residual violations on tight-constraint relations (Table~\ref{tab:composability}); adding S1 yields DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\% with no significant $\Delta$R-F1 (Bonferroni-corrected; 95\% CIs $\subseteq [-0.69, {+}0.25]$\,pp; removed triples are 97.6--100\% false positives; Appendix~\ref{app:downstream-impact}).
Under fine-tuning, grammar becomes a no-op ($\Delta$DR$<$0.2\,pp), making the semantic layer the sole DR defense (41--69\% on SciERC, 2--75\% on DocRED; Appendix~\ref{app:ft-ablation}); three relations with $\kappa \geq 0.36$ retain DR, all eliminated by S1 (Appendix~\ref{app:lora-per-relation}).
Fallback frequency is model-dependent: Qwen triggers 0 fallbacks under LoRA + S1 on SciERC, while Llama triggers 5{,}882 (Table~\ref{tab:ft-ablation}), reflecting weaker entity typing; despite this, DR reaches 0.09\% on SciERC (0.21\% on DocRED), confirming that even frequent fallback does not compromise enforcement (Appendix~\ref{app:llama-per-relation}).
CF drops from $+$9.82\,pp (zero-shot) to $+$1.18\,pp (fine-tuned), concentrated in \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X ambiguity (63.3\% of zero-shot CF; Appendix~\ref{app:cf-distribution}); beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types at 8B (R-F1 43--46; \S\ref{sec:beam-results}).

%  CF quantification (MF1 response)
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Cross-field violation analysis.}
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1 (ZS: CF=248, 167 docs), w5_lora_scierc_full_s1_eval (FT: CF=21, 20 docs)
Under zero-shot greedy S1, CF is the sole residual violation type (DR, RV, ET all eliminated): 248 violations across 167 documents, 63.3\% involving \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X type ambiguity (Appendix~\ref{app:cf-distribution}).
A source breakdown shows 58.1\% originate from hallucinated entities, while true cascade errors account for only 7.3\% (Appendix~\ref{app:cascade-analysis}); fine-tuning reduces CF to 1.18\% with cascade errors eliminated; beam $k{=}4$ eliminates all remaining CF (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).

1	% Section 3 — Method (Draft)
2	% OntoCoDec: Type-Valid Information Extraction
3	% via Compiled Ontology Constraints
4	
5	\section{Method}
6	\label{sec:method}
7	
8	\input{fig1_framework}
9	
10	We present OntoCoDec, a framework that translates IE ontologies into token-level constraints enforced during autoregressive generation.
11	The design is guided by a decidability analysis of IE type constraints.
12	
13	\paragraph{Constraint decidability taxonomy.}
14	\label{sec:decidability}
15	We classify IE type constraints into three levels: (1)~\emph{context-free}: vocabulary membership and JSON structure; (2)~\emph{prefix-decidable with state}: domain/range type validity, determined at each type-bearing position given the decoded relation type and entity registry; (3)~\emph{non-local}: cross-entity type consistency, which depends on the full output.
16	Unlike code generation where types are statically declared, IE constraints fall into level~2: entity types are inferred from text, the registry is built dynamically, and constraint targets depend on the co-occurring relation.
17	OntoCoDec enforces levels 1--2 (grammar and semantic layers, respectively); level~3 is addressed by beam search or post-hoc resolution (Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).
18	
19	\smallskip
20	\noindent
21	Existing grammar-constrained decoding frameworks (e.g., XGrammar) enforce level~1 constraints---structural validity and vocabulary membership---but IE domain/range rules require cross-position entity-type state that context-free grammars cannot express.
22	Even when the entity set is finite, encoding type constraints into a deterministic finite automaton (DFA) requires $O(|\mathcal{E}|^{|\text{entities}|})$ states: for typical SciERC documents (median 17 entities, 6 types), $6^{17} \approx 1.6{\times}10^{13}$ states; for DocRED (median 19 entities, 6 types), $6^{19} \approx 6.1{\times}10^{14}$---well beyond practical construction for online decoding.
23	While cross-reference binding is known to exceed context-free expressiveness in programming language theory, its implications for IE-specific type constraints---where entity types are inferred from text rather than statically declared---have not been formally characterized.
24	Formally, domain/range constraints for unbounded entity sets are not context-free (\textbf{Proposition~1}; proof via pumping argument in Appendix~\ref{app:pumping-lemma}): a pushdown automaton (PDA) cannot retrieve the type of entity $e_k$ without destroying stack entries above it.
25	OntoCoDec's semantic layer addresses this with a runtime entity registry $\mathcal{D}$ (a finite map enabling random-access type lookups), avoiding both the theoretical impossibility (unbounded) and the engineering intractability (finite but exponential).
26	
27	\noindent\textbf{Empirical Observation} (scale-dependent enabling dependency)\textbf{.} The grammar layer alone cannot enforce domain/range constraints (Proposition~1), while the semantic layer alone achieves only 24\% DR reduction at 8B without grammar-enforced vocabulary membership (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}, Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation}).
28	The strength of this dependency is scale-dependent: at 70B, the semantic layer independently achieves 84\% DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}), whereas 8B models show only 24\% independent reduction.
29	\smallskip
30	
31	We describe the problem formulation (\S\ref{sec:formulation}), each layer, and two decoding strategies (\S\ref{sec:strategies}); formal analysis of constraint composition is in Section~\ref{sec:composition}.
32	
33	
34	\subsection{Problem Formulation}
35	\label{sec:formulation}
36	
37	\paragraph{IE as structured generation.}
38	Given an input text $x$, a language model generates a structured JSON output $y$:
39	%
40	\begin{equation}\label{eq:output-schema}
41	\resizebox{.88\columnwidth}{!}{$\displaystyle
42	  y = \bigl\{\texttt{entities}: [\{n_i, \tau_i\}],\; \texttt{relations}: [\{h_j, t_j, r_j, \tau^h_j, \tau^t_j\}]\bigr\}
43	$}
44	\end{equation}
45	%
46	where each entity has a name $n_i$ and type $\tau_i \in \mathcal{E}$, and each relation specifies head $h_j$, tail $t_j$, relation type $r_j \in \mathcal{R}$, and head/tail entity types $\tau^h_j, \tau^t_j$.
47	The output JSON Schema (\S\ref{sec:grammar}) enforces a fixed field ordering (head $\to$ tail $\to$ relation $\to$ head\_type $\to$ tail\_type) via deterministic grammar compilation, ensuring the relation type $r_j$ is known before entity type fields and enabling sequential domain/range lookups (\S\ref{sec:dynamic-masking}).
48	The grammar structurally enforces entity-before-relation ordering (maintained in all documents across all configurations), ensuring the entity registry (\S\ref{sec:entity-registry}) is populated before relation-level type constraints are evaluated; unregistered entities trigger domain-only filtering.
49	
50	\paragraph{Ontology compliance.}
51	Using the ontology $\mathcal{O} = (\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{R}, \sigma)$ defined in \S\ref{sec:background}, we write $\operatorname{dom}(r) = \{\tau^h : \exists \tau^t,\, (\tau^h, \tau^t) \in \sigma(r)\}$ for domain-valid head types and $\operatorname{range}(r, \tau^h) = \{\tau^t : (\tau^h, \tau^t) \in \sigma(r)\}$ for the conditional range given head type $\tau^h$.
52	Our enforcement target is \emph{pair-based} type validity: $(\tau^h, \tau^t) \in \sigma(r)$ for every triple.
53	The decoder enforces this sequentially: $\tau^h \in \operatorname{dom}(r)$ at head position, then $\tau^t \in \operatorname{range}(r, \tau^h)$ at tail position, achieving best-effort pair-based enforcement (pair validity ensured when no fallback is triggered; domain-only filtering otherwise) strictly stronger than independent domain/range checks (which over-permit 33--37\% spurious pairs on SciERC/DocRED; \S\ref{sec:rectangularity}).
54	
55	
56	\subsection{Grammar Layer}
57	\label{sec:grammar}
58	
59	A JSON Schema encoding Eq.~\eqref{eq:output-schema} with \texttt{enum} constraints ($\mathcal{E}$, $\mathcal{R}$) is compiled into a pushdown automaton via XGrammar~\cite{dong2025xgrammar}.
60	At step $t$, grammar-valid tokens $G(t) \subseteq V$ pass; all others receive logits $-\infty$, enforcing structural validity, vocabulary membership ($r_j \in \mathcal{R}$, $\tau_i \in \mathcal{E}$), but not domain/range constraints (which depend on entity types within each triple).
61	
62	\subsection{Semantic Layer}
63	\label{sec:semantic}
64	
65	The semantic layer enforces domain/range constraints through a stateful logits processor maintaining an entity registry during generation.
66	\emph{Running example}: for \textsc{Used-for} ($\operatorname{dom}{=}\{\textrm{Method}\}$, $\operatorname{range}{=}\{\textrm{Task}\}$), entity ``ResNet'' (Method) passes the head-type check while Material is blocked; ``image classification'' (Task) passes the tail-type check.
67	
68	\paragraph{Entity registry.}
69	\label{sec:entity-registry}
70	The semantic layer builds a registry $\mathcal{D}: \text{name} \to \text{type}$ incrementally during entity generation: each completed entry $\{n_i, \tau_i\}$ adds $(n_i, \tau_i)$ to $\mathcal{D}$, which is consulted during relation generation for type lookups.
71	The registry uses \emph{first-seen} semantics: when an entity name appears in multiple triples, the type assigned at its first occurrence governs all subsequent constraint checks, making type enforcement sensitive to generation order.
72	At each step $t$, the processor pattern-matches the decoded prefix to identify the current field position; semantic masks activate only at type-bearing positions (\textsc{HeadType}, \textsc{TailType}).
73	\label{sec:position-detection}
74	
75	\paragraph{Dynamic masking.}
76	\label{sec:dynamic-masking}
77	At type-bearing positions, the processor computes a semantic mask $S(t) \subseteq V$.
78	At a \textsc{HeadType} position, if $h_j \in \mathcal{D}$ and $\mathcal{D}[h_j] \in \operatorname{dom}(r_j)$, the mask allows only the registered type; otherwise it falls back to all domain-valid types $\operatorname{dom}(r_j)$.
79	At a \textsc{TailType} position, the mask restricts to $\operatorname{range}(r_j, \tau^h_j)$ conditioned on the already-determined head type, further narrowing to the registered type when $t_j \in \mathcal{D}$.
80	This sequential check achieves best-effort pair-based enforcement (\S\ref{sec:formulation}), strictly tighter than independent domain/range checking; ``best-effort'' reflects the grammar-first fallback (\S\ref{sec:composition}), which prioritizes JSON integrity over type validity when constraints conflict.
81	
82	\paragraph{Tokenizer-agnostic type masking.}
83	We use \emph{continuation masking} to handle context-dependent tokenizations and prefix-shared types (e.g., \textsc{Sen}/\textsc{Sid}/\textsc{Side} in WikiEvents): a compile-time prefix map identifies valid continuations for each type name, disambiguating over multiple steps across byte-level byte pair encoding (BPE) (Qwen, Llama) and SentencePiece (Mistral).
84	
85	\paragraph{Grammar-semantic interaction.}
86	\label{sec:interaction}
87	The final mask is $G(t) \cap S(t)$; when empty, grammar-first fallback applies (\S\ref{sec:composition}), embodying this interaction: semantic constraints reduce DR by only 24\% without grammar-enforced vocabulary.
